clue.text: Felt sorry corralling horse that's difficult

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for an adjective

indicators.note: to corral animals is to pen them in, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: to rue is to feel regret
gee-gee is a childish word for a horse

explanation.surface: Someone regrets having to pen in a stubborn, awkward horse.
explanation.walkthrough: GG (gee-gee) is the nursery word for a horse, and the corral fits neatly into the horse picture. RUED opens to hold GG: RU-GG-ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugged terrain or a rugged task is hard going, so rugged describes something tough and demanding.

clue.text: Polish hero crossed by rebellious old Roman

definitions.note: a description of the river, standing for its name

parts.note: to polish something is to rub it
an icon is an idolised figure

explanation.surface: A Polish hero meets a rebellious ancient Roman who crosses him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital looks like the nationality, but it is the verb to shine. The 'rebellious old Roman' is Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar defied the Senate by leading his army over this small Italian river in 49 BC, starting a civil war.

clue.text: Odd ones in law court go back to complain

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction, right to left
the odd-numbered letters are the first, third, fifth and so on of the phrase

parts.note: letters 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 of the three words run together

explanation.surface: Strange people in a court of law go back to make a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd ones' sounds like eccentric people, but it means the odd-positioned letters. 'go' is part of the source, not a verb in the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To growl is to grumble or speak in an angry, complaining way, like a snarling dog.

clue.text: Rewrite an overdue essay

indicators.note: rewriting reworks text into a fresh arrangement of the same material

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A student is told to rewrite a homework essay handed in late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essay' looks like schoolwork; here it is the older sense of an attempt, as in 'essay a task'.
explanation.definitionFit: An essay, in its original meaning, is a try at doing something, which is exactly what an endeavour is.

clue.text: Sanctions mouthpiece for leak

parts.note: to sanction something is to permit it
a lip is part of the mouth; also cheeky talk

explanation.surface: A spokesperson is punished with sanctions for leaking information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sanctions' suggests penalties, but here it is the opposite sense, permits. 'mouthpiece' suggests a spokesperson, not a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: To let slip a secret is to reveal it accidentally, just as a leak passes on information that should stay hidden.

clue.text: Figure of speech child found in stories — that's an understatement

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, enclosed on both sides

parts.note: stories in the sense of fibs
a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: A child telling tall tales prompts a dry remark about understatement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stories' here are fibs, not tales. The closing phrase is a wry tag rather than wordplay: it describes what this figure of speech does.
explanation.definitionFit: Litotes is a rhetorical device using ironic understatement, such as saying 'not bad' to mean very good.

clue.text: Short piece from Pinter series

indicators.note: a piece taken from something is a fragment of it, so the letters sit inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A short play from a series by the playwright Harold Pinter.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinter is apt: his dialogue is famously clipped, so 'Short piece' reads naturally as a brief play.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse speech is brief and to the point, using few words, which is a sense of short.

clue.text: A girl they shifted some distance away

definitions.note: a phrase describing the answer, which is a noun

indicators.note: things shifted are moved around into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl's family moved house to somewhere quite far off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifted' reads as moved house, which suits 'some distance away', but it signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A light year is the distance light travels in a year, used as a unit for vast astronomical lengths.

clue.text: Exercise US prosecutor books? He'll still find fault with it

definitions.text: He'll still find fault with it

parts.note: physical education
district attorney
the New Testament books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A prosecutor works hard on the case, yet someone will nitpick anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition follows straight on from the wordplay: whatever the work, 'he'll still find fault with it'. NT for New Testament is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant fusses over minor details and rules, criticising tiny errors even in otherwise sound work.

clue.text: Game return of international staff

indicators.note: a return is a journey back the way one came

parts.note: an international sportsman earns a cap for playing for his country
to staff a desk is to man it

explanation.surface: A tennis match's return play, or the comeback of a company's overseas workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a player selected for the national team is 'capped', so a cap is an international. 'staff' is the verb, to MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Pac-Man is the classic 1980 arcade video game in which a yellow disc eats dots in a maze.

clue.text: Show second-rate players taking on course

indicators.note: to take something on is to take it in and hold it

parts.note: B grade is second class
the actors in a play
a road is a route or way

explanation.surface: A show staged by a mediocre troupe takes on a fresh direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second-rate players' is one piece split in two: the grade letter and the actors, with the course slotted between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast is a programme sent out on television or radio, which is a show.

clue.text: Firm hides soldier in shed

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits enclosed within it

parts.note: to shed something is to get rid of it
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A company is concealing a soldier in a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company and 'shed' like a hut; they are the adjective and the verb to discard.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rigid is stiff and unbending, which is one sense of firm.

clue.text: Back smart type of fellow to embrace independent woman

indicators.note: going back means running the letters in the opposite direction
an embrace wraps around, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a smart Alec is a know-all
abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Supporting a clever man who takes up with an independent-minded woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a verb meaning support, but it is the reversal signal. A smart Alec is a cocky know-it-all; ALEC holds I, then the whole is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Celia is a female given name, so any woman called that fits the general term.

clue.text: Doctors hate to interrupt men the worse for wear?

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so one piece splits another

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, altering its form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Medics dislike breaking in on men who have had too much to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like the subject noun but is the verb meaning tamper with; 'the worse for wear' suggests drunkenness, not shabby clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Moth-eaten clothes have holes chewed by moths, and the word extends to anything shabby and worn out.

clue.text: NB: it's just been delivered

parts.note: surface reading: a note that a parcel has just arrived
setter's reading: the two letters are the initials of a two-part description of a baby that has just been delivered

explanation.walkthrough: NB normally means 'note well' and 'delivered' suggests the post; but read NB as initials and 'delivered' as a baby's birth.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby just delivered by a midwife is a newborn infant, only hours or days old.

clue.text: Offensive type, comfortable with more extended line out

parts.note: snug and cosy

indicators.note: something out is gone, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: stretched further
abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A rude person makes themselves cosy and stretches out on the sofa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' suggests rude, but it is the military sense, keen to attack. LONGER loses its L.
explanation.definitionFit: A warmonger stirs up and favours armed conflict, so they are a person bent on going on the offensive.

clue.text: Leader castigated for holding back something so revered

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for an adjective

indicators.note: back means the letters are read in the opposite direction
words that hold something carry it inside them

parts.note: letters spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A leader is reprimanded for holding back on something treated as holy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'castigated' tempts a synonym hunt, but the answer lies within leaDER CAStigated, read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sacred is holy and treated with deep reverence, so it is described as revered.

clue.text: Evil caste circulating a stoical philosophy

indicators.note: something circulating moves around, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wicked social class spreads a philosophy of grim endurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase means 'that's life', said with a shrug when things go wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'that's life' accepts misfortune calmly without complaint, which is the core of Stoic thinking.

clue.text: Rehearsal for smuggling booze?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a practice before the real thing
second meaning, whimsical: a run (smuggling trip) of drink into a dry, alcohol-free territory

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: a run is a smuggling trip, and a 'dry' state or county bans alcohol, as in US Prohibition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry run is a trial performance to test that everything works before the actual event.

clue.text: Capture piece — it will secure things more quickly!

definitions.text: it will secure things more quickly

parts.note: to nail a criminal is to catch them
piece is slang for a firearm

explanation.surface: Take a chess piece and you will lock down your position faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capture piece' sounds like chess, but piece is gangster slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail gun drives nails in with compressed air, fastening timber far faster than a hammer.

clue.text: Grit sac evolved — it's involved in digestion

indicators.note: something evolved has developed into a changed form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird's gizzard, a sac for grit, developed to help it digest.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: many birds keep grit in a muscular pouch to grind food.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric means relating to the stomach, the organ where much of the breaking down of food happens.

clue.text: Arrive at hotel inside poor neighbourhood

indicators.note: one thing inside another is enclosed by it

parts.note: to arrive at a place is to get to it
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Checking into a hotel in a run-down part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: H for hotel comes from the radio alphabet (Alpha, Bravo ... Hotel). It goes inside GET TO.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghetto is a deprived, overcrowded urban district, often home to a minority group.

clue.text: Produce cover — it's certainly revealing

parts.note: a crop is farm produce
a top covers a container

explanation.surface: Putting a cover over farm produce, which nonetheless gives a lot away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' reads as a verb but is the noun for farm yield; 'revealing' means showing skin, not information.
explanation.definitionFit: A crop top is a short garment that stops above the waist, leaving the midriff bare.

clue.text: Plant at the heart of pagans' peerless medicine

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the central two of six letters
the central two of eight letters
the central two of eight letters

explanation.surface: A plant central to a heathen people's unrivalled folk remedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peerless' looks like a deletion of PEER, but it is just a word whose middle is wanted; the surface fits garlic's role in folk medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Garlic is a bulb-forming plant of the onion family, grown for its pungent cloves.

clue.text: Dealing so unexpectedly to get close

indicators.note: something done unexpectedly goes in a surprising way, so the order changes

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Doing business in a surprising way to clinch a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close' looks like the verb to finish a deal; it is the adverb, near.
explanation.definitionFit: Alongside means next to or beside, so something alongside is very near at hand.

clue.text: Courageous chap accommodating outsiders from Texas

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, so one piece is housed by another

parts.note: a guy is a man

indicators.note: the outsiders of a word are its edge letters, first and last

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A brave man takes in strangers who have come from Texas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outsiders' suggests strangers or newcomers, but it means the outer letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gutsy means showing guts, informal for nerve and bravery, so a gutsy person is brave.

clue.text: Brick producer limits time to fire

indicators.note: limits are boundaries on either side, so one piece is bounded by another

parts.note: the Danish maker of plastic toy bricks
abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A brickworks restricts the hours its kiln may be fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brick producer' suggests a brickworks and 'fire' a kiln; the producer is the toy company, and fire means dismiss.
explanation.definitionFit: To let an employee go is a euphemism for dismissing them from their job, the same as firing.

clue.text: Stuff leading tradesmen use removing paint stains

indicators.note: the leading part of a word is its front, so first letters are taken

parts.note: initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: The material that decorators use to remove paint marks.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes the answer itself: decorators clean brushes and paint spills with turpentine. TURPS is the informal British shortening.
explanation.definitionFit: Turps is a substance, a solvent liquid, so it is a kind of stuff or material.

clue.text: Run off in compliance with the rules

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang, to flee on foot (two words)
second meaning: informal for legal and above board

explanation.walkthrough: The split is LEG IT, British slang for running away; read whole, it is short for legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit, clipped from legitimate, describes something lawful and genuine that follows the regulations.

clue.text: Silly to grieve over time? Here's advice about moving on

indicators.note: something silly is foolish and muddled, so the letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: It is foolish to mourn for too long; here is some tough-love counsel.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes all nine letters, the time's T included. The surface and the answer agree: blunt advice to stop dwelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to get over it is blunt counsel urging them to stop dwelling on a loss and recover.

clue.text: Continue behaviour that started comedy film series

definitions.text: behaviour that started comedy film series
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a fuss or rowdy conduct, the phrase that begins every title of a long British film run

explanation.walkthrough: The Carry On films are a long-running series of bawdy British comedies (Carry On Nurse, Carry On Camping), every title starting with the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on is to proceed or keep going; as a noun, a carry-on is a commotion or fuss.

clue.text: Americans admit to making mistake when swapping female for male

indicators.note: a swap trades one thing for another, so a letter is exchanged

parts.note: a mess-up is a blunder
abbreviation for female
abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: Americans own up to having made an error by mixing up the sexes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Americans' marks the definition as US slang. In MESS UP the M (male) is replaced by F (female).
explanation.definitionFit: To fess up, from confess, is colloquial US English for owning up to a wrongdoing or error.
